doc.title: Ray Ricker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 27, 2022

title: Draft notice and winning a spot in the West Point band
summary: Finishing his master's at Michigan State, he got his draft notice and auditioned for the West Point band, then studied with Russianoff and Regni.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: I gleaned a lot of wonderful information from your book which we’ll get to. I understand the Vietnam war played a role in your decision about what direction to go when you were I guess late teens, early twenties?

Yeah well actually I was a little older than that because I think that was — I went in the Army in 1967. And I was there for three years, ’67 to ’70. But yeah, I was going to get drafted. And I already had, well I was finishing up my master’s degree at Michigan State and was getting ready to get married too. But my deferment, the day I got my degree, right after that I think it was on the weekend, on that Monday or Tuesday I got the “Welcome to the Army” draft notice. I went from 2S which was student, to 1A which was you’re at the top of the list and you’re going to get a physical. So I called a friend of mine who was in the West Point band and I said, “What’s going on at West Point? What’s going on there?” He says, “Oh it’s really a good thing, it’s 40 miles from New York and we go down and we take lessons in New York and work is not hard at all you’ve got a lot of free time and stuff and you go in as a rank of Sergeant and you get to stay there for three years.” I said, “Well man, how do I get into that?” He says, “You’ve got to audition.” He says, “I’ll see if there are any spots, if there’s going to be a spot coming up.” So he did, he checked it out, and sure enough there was, they said, “Come on and audition here in June” after I got my degree. So I did, I went there and it was not like it is today where you see an ad in the International Musician and they say, “Opening for clarinet.” It was more of not word-of-mouth so much but you had to be proactive and contact these different bands to find out if there was going to be anything coming up. And often they’d say no not yet, but I know there’s going to be a couple of clarinet players — or whatever you played — you know getting out within six months so maybe there will be then. So anyway I auditioned and I was successful with that and got in, and so they cut your papers right there and then you go to the recruiter and say, “Here’s where I’m going” you know and how do we do that. So you have to go through Basic Training. The only band that doesn’t go through Basic Training is the Marine band. Everybody else has to go through Basic. And so you know, did that, and then I was at West Point for three years. But it was great because I was taking lessons from Leon Russianoff in New York and the Army was paying for it, and I was also taking flute lessons from Albert Regni who was a well known studio player and commercial player in New York.
